view.stem: A mass $m$ of a fuel burns completely, releasing heat $Q$. Its calorific value is $q$. Which statements are correct? Select every correct statement.

options.text: Calorific value can be measured in $\mathrm{J/kg}$, $\mathrm{kcal/kg}$, or $\mathrm{cal/g}$.
Burning twice the mass of the same fuel gives the fuel twice the calorific value.
A fuel's calorific value describes the heat released by complete combustion of one kilogram of that fuel.
Calorific value can be measured in $\mathrm{J}$, $\mathrm{kcal}$, or $\mathrm{cal}$, with no mass denominator.
The released heat is $Q=qm$, with the mass unit in $m$ matching the mass unit in $q$.
The released heat is $Q=q/m$, with the mass unit in $m$ matching the mass unit in $q$.

intent.task: Identify the physical definition of calorific value, all three supplied energy-per-mass units, and the law relating fuel mass to total heat under complete combustion.
intent.source_solution: Block 6 defines q as heat released by complete combustion of 1 kg of the fuel. Block 7 supplies J/kg, kcal/kg and cal/g; 1 kcal/kg = 1 cal/g by cancellation of both kilo prefixes. Block 13 gives Q=qm with matching mass units, so (J/kg) kg gives J, (kcal/kg) kg gives kcal, and (cal/g) g gives cal. q is fuel-specific, while Q scales with sample mass. This unit-prefix equivalence does not assert an exact conversion between the table's independently rounded J and calorie columns.
intent.unit_reason: Sources 1, 2 and 4 are the coherent definition, dimensions and mass-scaling law for the same physical quantity. A native multiple response tests each substantive assertion directly without per-blank questions or combination-code options.
limitations: Recognition does not demonstrate independently writing the definition, listing the three units, or formulating the heat equation.
Selecting a supplied formula does not demonstrate a learner-produced dimensional derivation.

rationales.derivation: The three units in block 7 are energy per mass: J/kg, kcal/kg and cal/g. No numerical J-to-cal conversion is required.
For the same fuel q=Q/m. When mass becomes 2m, Q becomes 2qm, so q remains (2qm)/(2m)=q, not 2q.
rationales.misconception: Treat the sample's total heat as the fuel-specific calorific value: replace Q by q, apply the doubling rule Q(2m)=2Q(m), and conclude q doubles.

rationales.derivation: Complete combustion of 1 kg is precisely the normalization defining calorific value in block 6; the quantity is heat per unit mass, not total heat for any unspecified sample.
q=Q/m has dimensions energy/mass. J, kcal and cal alone measure Q, not q, so deleting the mass denominators changes the physical quantity.
rationales.misconception: Copy the units of total heat Q to the specific quantity q by dropping the /kg or /g denominator.

rationales.derivation: For a fuel with heat per mass q, multiplying by m gives Q=qm. Matching mass units cancel the denominator and leave an energy unit.
Starting with q=Q/m and multiplying both sides by m gives Q=qm. q/m instead has dimensions energy/mass squared and predicts decreasing heat with increasing mass.
rationales.misconception: When rearranging q=Q/m, divide q by m once more instead of multiplying by m, yielding the erroneous Q=q/m.

view.stem: A fuel's calorific value is reported as $1.4\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$ or $3400\ \mathrm{kcal/kg}$. The table also lists $10500$ for petroleum in its calorie-based column. Which statement correctly interprets both entries? The reported values are rounded.

options.text: Complete combustion of $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of the first fuel releases $1.4\times10^7\ \mathrm{J}$ or $3400\ \mathrm{kcal}$; petroleum's entry means $10500\ \mathrm{kcal/g}$.
Complete combustion of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the first fuel releases $1.4\times10^7\ \mathrm{J}$ or $3400\ \mathrm{kcal}$; petroleum's entry means $10500\ \mathrm{kcal/kg}$.
Complete combustion of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the first fuel releases $1.4\times10^7\ \mathrm{J}$ or $3400\ \mathrm{cal}$; petroleum's entry means $10500\ \mathrm{cal/kg}$.
Complete combustion of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of the first fuel releases $1.4\times10^7\ \mathrm{J}$ or $3400\ \mathrm{kcal}$; petroleum's entry means $10500\ \mathrm{J/kg}$.

intent.task: Interpret both numerical calorific-value quotations as heat released per specified fuel mass, retaining both reported values for the first fuel and the physical meaning and calorie-based unit of petroleum's 10500 entry.
intent.source_solution: For source 3, complete combustion of 1 kg releases the reported 1.4e7 J or separately reported 3400 kcal; the calorie reading is also 3400 cal/g. For g2-1, the table header makes petroleum's 10500 a value in kcal/kg or cal/g: 1 kg releases 10500 kcal, equivalently 1 g releases 10500 cal. The table's separate petroleum J-column entry is 4.4e7 J/kg. No exact conversion between these independently rounded columns is claimed.
intent.unit_reason: Sources 3 and g2-1 ask the same substantive per-mass interpretation for two different quotations. One complete paired interpretation preserves each quotation and petroleum's unit while avoiding two near-duplicate definition questions. It is not a selection of copied table values alone: sample mass, heat unit and per-mass unit must all be interpreted.
limitations: Recognition of a complete interpretation does not demonstrate independently composing an explanation or supplying a unit without alternatives.

The calorie-prefix equivalence cal/g versus kcal/kg is included in internal source solving, but the chosen correct complete statement expresses petroleum's entry in kcal/kg rather than requiring a separately written equivalent form.

The complete desktop rendering retains the rightmost header q (kcal/kg or cal/g), petroleum's 10500, peat's 1.4 x 10^7 and 3400, and the bottom hydrogen row. Mobile start/end panels show horizontal scrolling of the same full-width table. Actual pixels, not spec values, supply these source facts.

rationales.derivation: The denominator is kg. For 1 g=0.001 kg, the first fuel releases 1.4e4 J or 3.4 kcal, not 1.4e7 J or 3400 kcal. Petroleum's 10500 kcal/kg equals 10.5 kcal/g, not 10500 kcal/g.
rationales.misconception: Replace every kg denominator by g without dividing the numerical value by 1000, turning the 1 kg heat into a 1 g heat and 10500 kcal/kg into 10500 kcal/g.

rationales.derivation: Multiplying each first-fuel reported energy-per-kg value by 1 kg gives 1.4e7 J or 3400 kcal. Petroleum's 10500 is under the kcal/kg or cal/g header, so the stated kcal/kg reading gives 10500 kcal for complete combustion of 1 kg.
For 1 kg the calorie-column heat is 3400 kcal=3400000 cal, not 3400 cal. Petroleum's 10500 kcal/kg would be 10500000 cal/kg, not 10500 cal/kg.
rationales.misconception: Delete the kilo prefix from the energy unit without multiplying either numerical value by 1000.

rationales.derivation: The first-fuel interpretation is sound, but petroleum's 10500 belongs to the calorie column. Its independently reported J/kg value is 4.4e7, not 10500.
rationales.misconception: Read petroleum's rightmost numeric value but attach the middle column's J/kg header to it.

view.stem: Equal masses of dry firewood and the brown coal listed in the table burn completely under the same conditions. Which comparison of the heat released, together with its reason, is correct?

options.text: Dry firewood releases more heat: its calorific value is $1.0\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$, less than brown coal's $1.3\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$.
They release equal heat: their equal masses make the heat equal even though their calorific values differ.
Dry firewood releases more heat: its calorific value is $1.3\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$, greater than brown coal's $1.0\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$.
Brown coal releases more heat: its calorific value is $1.3\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$, greater than dry firewood's $1.0\times10^7\ \mathrm{J/kg}$.

intent.task: Compare total heat from the two fuels under controlled equal-mass and complete-combustion conditions, and identify calorific value as the quantitative basis.
intent.source_solution: For the same positive mass m, Q_brown=(1.3e7 J/kg)m and Q_wood=(1.0e7 J/kg)m, so brown coal releases more heat. The calorie column independently gives the same ordering, 3000>2500 kcal/kg. These rounded columns imply different approximate ratios, 1.3 and 1.2, which are not equated or requested. The source's phrase 'completely identical conditions' does not explicitly give equal masses; without equal masses the comparison is underdetermined. The visible stem therefore declares equal masses and complete combustion as the fair-comparison interpretation.
intent.unit_reason: The requested fuel comparison and its grounds form one physical judgment. Each option pairs a winner with a calorific-value basis, so recognizing a fuel name alone is insufficient.
limitations: Selecting a supplied comparison and reason does not demonstrate independently writing the argument Q=qm.

The stem explicitly clarifies equal mass and complete combustion; the written source's same-conditions phrase did not explicitly state these. The unclarified comparison for arbitrary unequal fuel masses is not claimed to be settled.

The current table SVG is 539a9c2c708fc126edeadf3221e1036c1097488491d5f5ef578ded74f3b7bbae. The visible dry-firewood row reads 1.0 x 10^7 J/kg and 2500 kcal/kg, and brown coal (Moscow region) reads 1.3 x 10^7 J/kg and 3000 kcal/kg. Both numerical columns, the right border and bottom hydrogen row are present in the complete desktop panel.

rationales.derivation: The quoted values are correctly assigned, but Q=qm is increasing in q for the same positive mass. Since 1.0e7<1.3e7, dry firewood releases less, not more, heat.
rationales.misconception: Use the inverse relation Q=m/q instead of Q=qm; equal m and smaller q then wrongly make dry firewood's heat larger.

rationales.derivation: Equal m does not cancel a difference in q: Q_brown-Q_wood=(1.3e7-1.0e7)m is positive, so the total heats are not equal.
rationales.misconception: Treat calorific value as universal or ignore it, replacing Q=qm by a common multiple of mass alone and concluding equal m implies equal Q.

rationales.derivation: The table assigns 1.0e7 J/kg to dry firewood and 1.3e7 J/kg to brown coal. The option swaps these row assignments, producing the opposite winner.
rationales.misconception: Interchange the two fuel-row labels before applying Q=qm, so the larger brown-coal value is incorrectly attributed to dry firewood.

rationales.derivation: Equal positive masses preserve the order of q in Q=qm. Brown coal's 1.3e7 J/kg exceeds dry firewood's 1.0e7 J/kg, so brown coal's heat is greater.

view.stem: How much heat is released by complete combustion of $15\ \mathrm{kg}$ of charcoal and of $200\ \mathrm{g}$ of alcohol? Each listed result uses the table's J/kg column or, separately, its kcal/kg column; the two columns are independently rounded.

intent.task: Calculate both requested complete-combustion heat quantities, retaining 15 kg charcoal, 200 g alcohol, fuel-specific calorific values and explicit energy units in a complete paired result.
intent.source_solution: Charcoal: 15 kg times 3.4e7 J/kg gives 5.1e8 J; the separate calorie column gives 15 times 8000=120000 kcal. Alcohol: 200 g=0.200 kg, so 0.200 times 2.7e7=5.4e6 J; independently 0.200 times 6500=1300 kcal. With cal/g this is 200 times 6500=1300000 cal. The J and kcal totals come from their respective rounded source columns, not an imported conversion constant or a claim of exact equivalence.
intent.unit_reason: The written task requests two named-fuel heat totals. One complete paired result retains both quantitative parts and tests fuel matching, mass scaling and grams-to-kg conversion without turning each value or unit into a separate arithmetic click.
limitations: Selecting both completed calculations does not demonstrate independently producing or documenting the multi-step arithmetic and unit conversion.
The correct option retains both J-column and kcal-column results; a separately written equivalent alcohol result in cal is not required.

figure_observations.observation: Opened the actual original table PNG and the complete modern native screenshot. The alcohol row reads 2.7 x 10^7 J/kg and 6500 kcal/kg or cal/g; charcoal reads 3.4 x 10^7 J/kg and 8000 kcal/kg or cal/g. The full desktop panel includes all twelve rows, the rightmost calorie column and bottom border, matching the current SVG hash 539a9c2c708fc126edeadf3221e1036c1097488491d5f5ef578ded74f3b7bbae. No modern conversion constant or data from a solution artifact was used.

rationales.derivation: The alcohol calculation is correct, but 3.4e7 J and 8000 kcal are the charcoal values for 1 kg. For 15 kg, multiplying each by 15 gives 5.1e8 J and 120000 kcal.
rationales.misconception: Omit the charcoal mass factor in Q=qm, reporting its one-kilogram table values as the total for 15 kg.

rationales.derivation: The charcoal calculation is correct. Multiplying alcohol's per-kg values by 200 yields 5.4e9 J and 1300000 kcal, but the given 200 g is 0.200 kg, so these totals are 1000 times too large.
rationales.misconception: Insert the numeric gram mass 200 into a formula using J/kg and kcal/kg without converting grams to kilograms.

rationales.derivation: Charcoal: 15 times 3.4e7=5.1e8 J, separately 15 times 8000=120000 kcal. Alcohol: 200/1000=0.200 kg, then 0.200 times 2.7e7=5.4e6 J and separately 0.200 times 6500=1300 kcal.
The alcohol calculation is correct. Erroneously replacing 15 kg by 15/1000=0.015 kg gives charcoal heat 0.015 times 3.4e7=5.1e5 J and 0.015 times 8000=120 kcal, rather than the required 15 kg totals.
rationales.misconception: Apply grams-to-kilograms division by 1000 to charcoal even though its mass is already stated in kilograms.
